mcq.q: A stack follows which access rule?
mcq.e: Last In First Out.

mcq.q: Where do all additions and removals of a stack take place?
mcq.e: Both push and pop are restricted to the top.

mcq.q: Overflow happens when:
mcq.e: Overflow = push on full.

mcq.q: Underflow happens when:
mcq.e: Underflow = pop from empty.

mcq.q: In an array-based stack, which value of top means the stack is empty?
mcq.e: top starts at -1.

mcq.q: In an array-based stack of size 10, the stack is full when top equals:
mcq.e: top = size - 1.

mcq.q: push in the array-based stack does:
mcq.e: Move top up first, then store.

mcq.q: pop in the array-based stack does:
mcq.e: Read the item, then move top down.

mcq.q: After push(5), push(7), push(9), pop(), what is on top?
mcq.e: 9 is removed, 7 is now on top.

mcq.q: Input A, B, C is pushed, then everything is popped and printed. Output:
mcq.e: LIFO reverses the order.

mcq.q: The destroy() operation of the array-based stack:
o: Releases the memory of the array
mcq.e: RELEASE MEMORY[] p.

mcq.q: Why must the array-based stack choose a capacity in advance?
o: Arrays have a predefined maximum capacity, fixed once allocated
mcq.e: Even dynamic arrays have a fixed capacity after allocation.

mcq.q: Which problem do linked list-based stacks avoid?
mcq.e: Linked nodes grow and shrink dynamically.

mcq.q: In a linked list-based stack the bottom node's next pointer is:
mcq.e: The end of the chain is null.

mcq.q: In a linked stack, the stack is empty when:
mcq.e: isEmpty tests top = null.

mcq.q: Linked push begins with p <- top. Why?
o: To save the old top so the new node can point to it
mcq.e: Without saving it the rest of the stack would be lost.

mcq.q: In linked pop, why is p <- top done before top <- top->next?
o: To keep the node so it can be released afterwards
mcq.e: p remembers the node to RELEASE MEMORY.

mcq.q: In C++ what does p[++top] = d; do?
o: Stores at the old top, then increments
Increments top, then stores at the new top
mcq.e: Pre-increment.

mcq.q: In C++ d = p[top--]; does:
o: Reads the top item, then decrements top
mcq.e: Post-decrement.

mcq.q: What is the effect of int pop(char &d) using a reference parameter?
o: Assigning to d changes the caller's variable
mcq.e: It is the REF of the pseudocode.

mcq.q: What does the destructor ~stack() correspond to in the pseudocode?
mcq.e: Constructor = create, destructor = destroy.

mcq.q: Which application would you NOT normally implement with a stack?
o: Serving print jobs in the order received
mcq.e: First come first served is a queue (FIFO).

mcq.q: To convert 25 to binary using a stack, the bits pushed (first to last) are:
In bracket checking, a closing bracket arrives and the stack is empty. Result:
mcq.e: The pop fails: no matching opener.

mcq.q: At the end of bracket checking the stack is not empty. Result:
mcq.e: A leftover opening bracket has no closer.

mcq.q: Postfix expression 12+34+*= evaluates to:
When an operator is read in postfix evaluation, which operand is popped first?
mcq.e: The first pop is the right-hand operand (operand2).

mcq.q: Evaluate the postfix expression 53-=
mcq.e: operand2 = 3, operand1 = 5: 5 - 3 = 2.

mcq.q: What data structure suits evaluating a postfix expression?
mcq.e: Operands are held until an operator pops them.

mcq.q: Complexity of push and pop on a stack is:
mcq.e: A constant number of steps regardless of stack size.

written.q: Define a stack and state its access rule, operations and error conditions.
written.a: A stack is a linear data structure in which all data additions (push) and removals (pop) are restricted to one end, the top. Access rule: Last In First Out (LIFO). Operations: push() and pop() (plus create, destroy, isEmpty and, array-based, isFull). Error conditions: overflow (pushing onto a full stack) and underflow (popping from an empty stack).

written.q: Write the pseudocode for create, push and pop of an array-based stack.
written.a:
ALGORITHM create(VAL s INTEGER)
1 size ← s
2 top ← -1
3 p ← ALLOCATE MEMORY DATATYPE[size]
END create

ALGORITHM push(VAL d DATATYPE)
1 IF (isFull())
2    RETURN false
3 ELSE
4    top ← top + 1
5    p[top] ← d
6    RETURN true
7 END IF
END push

ALGORITHM pop(REF d DATATYPE)
1 IF (isEmpty())
2    RETURN false
3 ELSE
4    d ← p[top]
5    top ← top - 1
6    RETURN true
7 END IF
END pop

isFull: top = size − 1. isEmpty: top = −1.

written.q: Write the push and pop algorithms of a linked list-based stack and explain why no isFull is needed.
written.a:
ALGORITHM push(VAL d DATATYPE)
1 p ← top
2 top ← ALLOCATE MEMORY node
3 top->data ← d
4 top->next ← p
END push

ALGORITHM pop(REF d DATATYPE)
1 IF (isEmpty())
2    RETURN false
3 ELSE
4    d ← top->data
5    p ← top
6    top ← top->next
7    RELEASE MEMORY p
8    RETURN true
9 END IF
END pop

No isFull is needed because each push allocates a new node, so the stack has no fixed capacity.

written.q: Compare array-based and linked list-based stacks.
written.a: The array-based stack needs a predefined maximum capacity (fixed at compile time for static arrays; fixed after allocation for dynamic arrays) even if the whole capacity is not used, so it wastes memory in most cases and can overflow. The linked list-based stack grows and shrinks dynamically at run time, using memory only for the items present (plus one pointer per node). Both give O(1) push and pop.

written.q: Write an algorithm that reads a postfix expression ended by '=' and prints its value. Evaluate 12+34+*=.
written.a:
Use an integer stack. Read characters until '='. If the character is an operator: operand2 ← pop, operand1 ← pop, push (operand1 operator operand2). Otherwise convert the digit to an integer and push it. At '=' pop and print the result (assuming single-digit operands and a valid expression).

12+34+*=: push 1, 2; '+' gives 3; push 3, 4; '+' gives 7; '*' pops 7 and 3 and pushes 21; prints 21.

written.q: Write an algorithm using a stack to check an expression for bracket mismatch.
written.a: Push each '(' ; on ')' try to pop: if the pop fails (empty stack) return false; at the end of the expression, if the stack still holds an item (a pop succeeds) return false, otherwise true. See the isBracketOk pseudocode in the lesson.

written.q: Explain with an algorithm how a stack converts a decimal number to binary. Show 25.
written.a: Repeat: bit ← n MOD 2; push bit; n ← n / 2 until n = 0. Then pop and print each bit. The bits are generated least-significant first and the stack reverses them. For 25: pushed 1, 0, 0, 1, 1; popped output 11001.
